what_it_does: Sparse matrix multiplication — multiplying two matrices where most entries are zero, so only a small fraction of positions need actual computation — is a core operation in graph analysis, graph neural networks, and scientific simulation. Standard GPU code handles it poorly because the irregular pattern of non-zero entries leads to unpredictable memory accesses and leaves most of the GPU's math units idle. RTSpMSpM observes a surprising structural similarity between this problem and ray tracing (the technique used in realistic graphics to simulate how light bounces): both involve efficiently finding which pairs of items 'intersect' among a huge number of possibilities. Modern GPUs already have dedicated hardware units (RT cores) for ray-triangle intersection tests, normally used only for graphics. The authors first implement a proof-of-concept that maps sparse matrix multiplication onto the ray tracing API, then design an enhanced version that uses those same intersection units to also compute the actual arithmetic products simultaneously, adding only a tiny extra sliver of chip area (0.2%) to get significant speed improvements.
